title: PKCE with the S256 challenge method is mandatory on every authorisation-code exchange
description: Every authorisation redirect includes `code_challenge` derived from a cryptographically random 43-to-128-character `code_verifier` by BASE64URL(SHA256(verifier)), and `code_challenge_method=S256`. The `plain` challenge method is not accepted. The `code_verifier` is stored server-side on the pending-flow record keyed by `state`; it is never sent on the front channel and is never rendered into the client tier. The token exchange POST carries the `code_verifier` verbatim; the flow controller refuses to construct a token-exchange request that does not carry a matching verifier for the pending flow, and refuses to consume a token-exchange response for a `state` whose stored verifier does not match. A provider that refuses the S256 challenge method or that does not appear to enforce PKCE binding at all is a project-level ADR conversation, not a config-flag flip.
rationale: The authorisation-code flow without PKCE lets an attacker who intercepts an authorisation code (through a compromised redirect handler, a shared browser environment, or an intermediary proxy) redeem it at the token endpoint without further evidence of possession. PKCE binds the code to a verifier the requester holds; without the verifier the code is unspendable. Mandating S256 excludes the `plain` method that a mis-implemented provider might otherwise accept and that erodes the guarantee to nil.
